name: The Revelation Principle
statement: Anything a clever mechanism can achieve, a simple honest one can achieve too, where telling the truth is the best strategy.
statementAccent: telling the truth is the best strategy
meaning: The revelation principle is a foundational result in mechanism design stating that anything achievable by some mechanism, in some equilibrium, is also achievable by a direct mechanism in which players simply report their private information truthfully and truth-telling is itself an equilibrium, yielding the same outcome. Its practical payoff is enormous: instead of searching the boundless space of every conceivable auction, contract, or bargaining game, a theorist can restrict attention, without loss of generality, to the tractable class of incentive-compatible, truthful, direct-revelation mechanisms. Whatever any elaborate game can accomplish, some report-your-type-honestly scheme can accomplish too.
mechanism: The trick is to fold the strategising into the mechanism itself. Any manipulation a player would perform in the original game, choosing bids or messages cleverly, can be simulated by a new mechanism that asks each player only to report their type and then internally plays that player's original equilibrium strategy on their behalf. Since the player could do no better than their equilibrium strategy in the old game, they can do no better than reporting truthfully in the new one, so honesty is made optimal. The principle comes in two versions: a dominant-strategy form, where truth-telling is a dominant strategy, and a Bayesian-Nash form, where it is optimal in expectation given beliefs and others' honesty.

examples.text: Roger Myerson derived the revenue-maximising auction entirely within the space of truthful direct mechanisms, using the principle to avoid searching over every possible auction format.
In principal-agent and regulation problems, the designer can look only at truthful menus, reducing the search to incentive-compatibility and participation constraints.
A new mechanism that takes each player's reported type and plays their old equilibrium strategy for them makes lying pointless, since the mechanism already does what the player would have done.

variants.name: Dominant-strategy version
variants.text: Associated with Allan Gibbard's 1973 work: any social choice function implementable in dominant strategies is truthfully implementable in dominant strategies, the stronger and more demanding form.

variants.name: Bayesian-Nash version
variants.text: Generalised in the late 1970s by Myerson, Dasgupta, Hammond, and Maskin, and Holmström: to every Bayesian-Nash equilibrium corresponds a truthful direct mechanism with the same outcome.

whyItMatters: The revelation principle is the workhorse simplification of modern mechanism design, auction theory, and contract theory, letting economists characterise what outcomes are attainable by examining only truthful direct mechanisms rather than an unbounded universe of institutions. It underlies Myerson's optimal auction, the analysis of regulation, optimal taxation, and public-goods provision, and it was part of the body of work recognised by the 2007 Nobel prize in economics awarded to Leonid Hurwicz, Eric Maskin, and Roger Myerson for founding mechanism design theory. It turns an impossible search into a tractable one.

working.text: when hunting for an optimal design, search only incentive-compatible direct mechanisms, since they achieve any outcome the general ones can.
recognise that a mechanism can play a player's own best strategy for them, leaving honesty with nothing to gain.
distinguish the demanding dominant-strategy form from the weaker Bayesian-Nash form, which covers a larger class of achievable outcomes.

limits: The principle holds under idealising assumptions and weakens when they break. It requires full commitment by the designer, who must credibly not re-optimise after reports; with limited commitment or renegotiation it can fail. It assumes no collusion, so coalitional deviations can make truthful direct mechanisms non-optimal, and it assumes costless, unrestricted communication, so communication or complexity constraints undermine it. It is a static, single-stage result that needs care in dynamic settings, and it guarantees only that truth-telling is an equilibrium, not the unique one, which is exactly why the separate and harder problem of implementation exists. It is an equivalence result, not a claim that real institutions are direct mechanisms.
misreadings: It does not mean honesty is always the best policy for people in the world; it says a mechanism can be designed so truth-telling is an equilibrium yielding a given outcome. It does not imply real institutions should be direct report-your-type schemes, since indirect mechanisms like ascending auctions may be preferred for robustness or simplicity. It does not guarantee truth-telling is the unique equilibrium, which is why implementation theory is a distinct question. And it was not the invention of any single person, nor was the 2007 Nobel awarded for it specifically: Gibbard supplied the dominant-strategy version, several authors the Bayesian one, and the prize honoured mechanism design broadly.
origin: Originating with Allan Gibbard's 1973 dominant-strategy result and generalised to Bayesian settings in the late 1970s by Roger Myerson, Partha Dasgupta, Peter Hammond, Eric Maskin, and Bengt Holmström; central to the mechanism-design theory recognised by the 2007 Nobel prize.
